To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The bootstrap simulation technique provides a powerful tool for quantification of both variability and uncertainty for emission factors and other parameters of air pollution inventories.

(1) Bootstrap simulation is a powerful technique for quantifying both variability and uncertainty for emissions from stationary sources, and (2) a prototype software tool for quantification of uncertainty and variability in emission inventories has been developed, which can provide a basis for improved policy decisions.
the bootstrap simulation technique is a powerful tool for the quantification and characterization of both variability in emissions and uncertainty in inventories.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the application of a probabilistic approach for the quantification and characterization of variability and uncertainty in emissions inventories.
the development of a prototype tool for the quantification and display of variability and uncertainty in stationary source emission inventory data.
the development of methods and tools for the quantification and display of variability and uncertainty in emissions inventories.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the methodology described in this paper provides a powerful tool for quantification of variability in emissions from individual sources and uncertainty in emission inventory results, which in turn can be used for a variety of purposes, including development of emission reduction strategies.

the methodology and software tool developed for this work are capable of characterizing both variability (i.e. differences from one source to the next) and uncertainty (i.e. lack of knowledge regarding true emissions due to measurement errors, statistical random sampling error, and non-representative sampling) in emissions from a large group of sources.
this methodology is a valuable tool for characterizing the uncertainty and variability in emissions from stationary source inventories, but that the results should be viewed with caution.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated that it is possible to develop probabilistic emission inventories for criteria pollutants.

the use of bootstrap simulations and related techniques for quantification of variability, uncertainty, and error in emission factors can provide a powerful tool for improving the credibility of emission inventories.
the use of bootstrap simulations and related techniques for characterizing uncertainty and variability can be applied to emission factors, activity factors, and other inputs to emission inventories.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a probabilistic approach to emission inventory estimation is feasible and can be useful in many contexts, including the evaluation of the impacts of emission controls and in the development and implementation of emission trading schemes.
the use of probabilistic emission inventories will enable a more robust assessment of emission reduction strategies.
the use of bootstrap techniques to quantify both variability and uncertainty is feasible and practical.
